dmm-2013-relay-01.title: Residues mod 7
dmm-2013-relay-01.body:
This is problem 1A of the relay round; its answer $7$ is passed on to problem 1B.

The offsets $0,4,6,10,12,16,22$ leave the remainders $0,4,6,3,5,2,1$ modulo $7$, which are all different, so exactly one of the seven numbers is divisible by $7$. A prime divisible by $7$ equals $7$. If $n+k=7$ with $k\in\{0,4,6\}$ then $n\in\{7,3,1\}$; $n=1$ is not prime and $n=3$ gives $3+6=9$, not prime. So $n=7$, and indeed $7,11,13,17,19,23,29$ are all prime.

**Answer: 7**

dmm-2013-relay-02.title: One free choice per residue class
dmm-2013-relay-02.body:
This is problem 1B of the relay round (with $k=7$, the answer of problem 1A); its answer $128$ is passed on to problem 1C.

Integers fall into $k$ residue classes mod $k$, and the condition only links consecutive members $m,m+k$ of a class, which must alternate in colour. So in each class the colouring is determined by the colour of one member (two choices), and the classes are independent. The number of colourings is $2^k=2^7=128$.

**Answer: 128**

dmm-2013-relay-03.title: Recurrence for binary partitions
dmm-2013-relay-03.body:
This is problem 1C of the relay round (with $n=\frac{128}8=16$, using the answer $128$ of problem 1B).

Let $b(m)$ be the number of such sums for $m$ ($b(0)=1$). A sum for an odd number contains a $1$; removing one $1$ gives a bijection with sums for $m-1$, so $b(2j+1)=b(2j)$. A sum for $2j$ either contains a $1$ (remove one: $b(2j-1)$ ways) or has only even parts (halve every part: $b(j)$ ways). So $b(2j)=b(2j-1)+b(j)$.

$b(0..16)=1,1,2,2,4,4,6,6,10,10,14,14,20,20,26,26,36$, in particular $b(16)=b(15)+b(8)=26+10=36$.

**Answer: 36**

dmm-2013-relay-04.title: Outer faces plus tunnel walls
dmm-2013-relay-04.body:
This is problem 2A of the relay round; its answer $72$ is passed on to problem 2B.

The outside: each of the $6$ faces has area $9$ with a $1\times1$ hole removed, so $6\cdot8=48$.

The inside: the three tunnels meet in the central unit cube, which is removed entirely, and its six faces open onto the six tunnel arms. Each of the six arms (one unit cube long, between the centre and a face) has $4$ walls of area $1$, so $6\cdot4=24$. No other surface is exposed.

Total: $48+24=72$.

**Answer: 72**

dmm-2013-relay-05.title: Bayes' theorem
dmm-2013-relay-05.body:
This is problem 2B of the relay round (with $k=\frac{72}8=9$, using the answer $72$ of problem 2A); its answer is passed on to problem 2C.

There are $k+1=10$ coins, each equally likely to be picked. A fair coin gives five heads with probability $\frac1{32}$, the two-headed coin with probability $1$. So
$$P(\text{fair}\mid5\text{ heads})=\frac{\frac9{10}\cdot\frac1{32}}{\frac9{10}\cdot\frac1{32}+\frac1{10}\cdot1}=\frac{9/32}{9/32+1}=\frac9{41}.$$

(One printed version of the problem uses $k=72$ directly, which would give $\frac{72}{72+32}=\frac9{13}$.)

**Answer: $\frac9{41}$**

dmm-2013-relay-06.title: Largest square in a regular hexagon
dmm-2013-relay-06.body:
This is problem 2C of the relay round (with $s=\frac9{41}$, the answer of problem 2B).

For a hexagon of side $1$ place the centre at the origin with two sides horizontal; the hexagon is $|y|\le\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\sqrt3|x|+|y|\le\sqrt3$. A square centred at the origin with sides parallel to the axes and half-side $a$ fits iff its corner $(a,a)$ satisfies both: $a\le\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $(\sqrt3+1)a\le\sqrt3$, i.e. $a\le\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3+1}=\frac{3-\sqrt3}2$ (the stronger condition). So the side is $2a=3-\sqrt3\approx1.268$. (Checking rotated squares numerically shows no larger square fits.)

For side $s$ the largest square has side $(3-\sqrt3)s$, which for $s=\frac9{41}$ is $\frac{9(3-\sqrt3)}{41}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{9(3-\sqrt3)}{41}$**
